meta.intro: Built from the cases covered on the show — timelines, evidence, and the details most people miss. New quizzes drop automatically.

quizzes.title: The Watts Case: What You Really Know
quizzes.description: You've heard the headline version. Let's see how well you know what the evidence actually shows in the Watts family murders.

questions.q: What was Chris Watts's occupation at the time of the murders in August 2018?
questions.explain: Watts worked for Anadarko Petroleum as an operator. That job gave him access to the oil site in Weld County, Colorado — which became central to where investigators found Shanann, Bella, and Celeste.

questions.q: How did Shanann Watts's friend first raise the alarm on August 13, 2018?
options: She called 911 after finding the front door open
She contacted police after Shanann missed a scheduled flight
She called a neighbor when Shanann didn't answer repeated texts and calls after returning home
She reported Shanann missing at her workplace
questions.explain: Shanann had just returned from a work trip. Her friend Nickole Atkinson drove to the house, got no answer at the door, and contacted police directly. That welfare check set the whole investigation in motion within hours.

questions.q: Chris Watts initially gave a televised interview before his arrest. What did he claim in that appearance?
options: He said he had no knowledge of where his family was
He said Shanann had driven away with the girls after an argument
He said he suspected a stranger had entered the home
He refused to speak on camera
questions.explain: In that interview, Watts told a local news crew that he last saw Shanann leaving the house with the children after a heated conversation. Investigators were already reviewing surveillance footage and phone data that contradicted that account.

questions.q: Where were the remains of Bella and Celeste Watts discovered?
options: In shallow graves on a neighbor's property
Submerged in oil tanks at an Anadarko work site
Buried in a field near the family home
In the bed of Chris Watts's work truck
questions.explain: This is the detail that never leaves you once you read the case file. The girls were found in crude oil tanks at the Cervi 319 work site — a location Watts had visited that same morning, which investigators confirmed through his company GPS records.

questions.q: Chris Watts initially faced trial but ultimately pleaded guilty. What sentence did he receive?
options: Death penalty after a jury trial
Three consecutive life sentences without the possibility of parole
Life with the possibility of parole after 25 years
questions.explain: By pleading guilty in November 2018, Watts avoided the death penalty. The plea deal was accepted in part at the request of Shanann's family, who wanted to be spared a trial. He is serving five consecutive life terms — three for the murders, plus additional counts.

quizzes.title: The Moscow Student Murders
quizzes.description: You've heard the headlines. Here's what the case file actually shows. Four students, one house, one night. Let's see what you know.

questions.q: On what date were the four University of Idaho students killed in Moscow, Idaho?
questions.explain: The killings happened in the early morning hours of November 13, 2022. That date matters because it shapes the entire timeline investigators had to reconstruct — phone data, witness accounts, and surveillance footage all anchor to that night.

questions.q: What weapon did investigators say was used in the killings, according to the probable cause affidavit?
questions.explain: The affidavit specifies a fixed-blade knife. That detail drove a major part of the investigation — investigators publicly asked the public for information about Ka-Bar-style knives, and a sheath recovered at the scene became critical physical evidence.

questions.q: How many of the six housemates were NOT killed that night?
questions.explain: Two other roommates were in the house that night and survived. According to the affidavit, one of them briefly encountered a figure described as a masked man before retreating to her room. Their accounts were central to the early investigation.

questions.q: Bryan Kohberger, the man charged with the murders, was a graduate student studying what subject at Washington State University?
questions.explain: Kohberger was a Ph.D. student in criminology at WSU, located in Pullman, Washington — roughly ten miles from the victims' house in Moscow, Idaho. That proximity became one of the earliest focal points once investigators identified him as a suspect.

questions.q: Where was Kohberger arrested in late December 2022?
questions.explain: Kohberger was arrested at his parents' home in Allentown, Pennsylvania, where he had traveled over the holiday break. The arrest came after weeks of investigation that included cell phone data, DNA from the knife sheath, and vehicle surveillance footage.

quizzes.title: The Watts Case File
quizzes.description: Five questions on the 2018 Watts family case — the timeline, the interview, and the evidence. Covered in our Watts Family Murders episode.

questions.q: The Watts family murders took place in August 2018 in which Colorado town?
questions.explain: The family lived in Frederick, Colorado — a small town north of Denver in Weld County.

questions.q: What happened during Chris Watts' August 15 police interview?
options: He refused to speak without a lawyer
He failed a polygraph, then confessed
questions.explain: Watts failed a polygraph examination and, confronted with the results, began confessing shortly after.

questions.q: Where were the bodies of Shanann and the girls recovered?
questions.explain: They were recovered at an oil site where Watts had worked — Shanann in a shallow grave, the girls in oil tanks.

questions.q: What sentence did Chris Watts receive after pleading guilty?
questions.explain: In November 2018 he received multiple consecutive life sentences without the possibility of parole; prosecutors took death off the table as part of the plea.

questions.q: What made the case unravel so quickly for Watts?
options: His own TV interviews and inconsistencies
questions.explain: His on-camera pleas and shifting story drew immediate suspicion — investigators noted the inconsistencies within days, alongside neighbor surveillance footage.

quizzes.title: JonBenét: Just the Facts
quizzes.description: The 1996 Boulder case is buried in myth. Five questions on what's actually documented — from our JonBenét Ramsey episodes.

questions.q: In what city and year was JonBenét Ramsey found dead in her family home?
questions.explain: She was found on December 26, 1996, in the family's home in Boulder, Colorado.

questions.q: What was discovered in the home before her body was found?
questions.explain: An unusually long handwritten ransom note — about two and a half pages — was found on the kitchen staircase.

questions.q: The ransom note demanded $118,000. Why is that number significant?
options: It matched John Ramsey's recent bonus
questions.explain: The amount closely matched a bonus John Ramsey had received that year — one of the case's strangest details.

questions.q: Where in the house was JonBenét found?
questions.explain: Her father found her in a small basement room during a walkthrough of the house hours after police arrived.

questions.q: What is the official status of the case today?
questions.explain: Nearly three decades on, the case remains open and unsolved, with periodic new rounds of DNA testing.

quizzes.title: Cold Case IQ
quizzes.description: Evidence, forensics, and investigation fundamentals — how much detective do you actually have in you?

questions.q: Locard's exchange principle — the foundation of forensic science — says what?
options: The simplest explanation is usually right
questions.explain: Edmond Locard's principle: a perpetrator brings something to a crime scene and leaves with something from it. Every contact leaves a trace.

questions.q: Forensic genetic genealogy — the technique behind the Golden State Killer arrest — matches crime-scene DNA against what?
questions.explain: Investigators upload crime-scene DNA profiles to public genealogy databases like GEDmatch and build family trees toward a suspect.

questions.q: Why do investigators talk about the 'first 48 hours'?
options: Legal deadline to charge a suspect
Evidence and memories degrade fast — solve odds drop sharply after
questions.explain: Physical evidence, witness memory, and digital trails are freshest early — the odds of clearance drop significantly once the first days pass.

questions.q: In the 2017 Delphi case, what crucial evidence did victim Libby German leave investigators?
options: Video and audio of the suspect on her phone
questions.explain: Libby recorded video and audio of the man on the Monon High Bridge — evidence investigators called unprecedented, captured by the victim herself.

questions.q: What is NamUs?
options: A national database for missing and unidentified persons
questions.explain: The National Missing and Unidentified Persons System — a public national database that helps connect missing persons cases with unidentified remains.

quizzes.title: The Menendez File
quizzes.description: Beverly Hills, 1989 — five questions on the case from our Erik and Lyle episode. The record is stranger than the retellings.

questions.q: Where were Jose and Kitty Menendez killed in August 1989?
questions.explain: Both were shot in the den of the family's Beverly Hills mansion on Elm Drive — a house later sold, and avoided, by buyers who knew the file.

questions.q: How did investigators first tie the brothers to a confession?
questions.explain: Sessions with psychologist Dr. Jerome Oziel were recorded — the fight over those tapes went all the way to the California Supreme Court.

questions.q: What happened at the brothers' first trials in 1993-94?
questions.explain: Each brother had his own jury. Both deadlocked — jurors split largely along lines of how they read the abuse testimony.

questions.q: The 1996 retrial ended with what sentence?
questions.explain: Convicted of first-degree murder with special circumstances, both received life without the possibility of parole.

questions.q: Where did the brothers buy the shotguns?
questions.explain: They drove south and bought the shotguns at a Big 5 in San Diego, using a borrowed ID — a detail the prosecution leaned on for premeditation.

quizzes.title: Delphi: The Evidence
quizzes.description: The 2017 Monon High Bridge case, from our Delphi episode — what the recording, the round, and the timeline actually established.

questions.q: What did Libby German capture on her phone that investigators called unprecedented?
options: A photo of a license plate
Video and audio of the suspect
questions.explain: Libby recorded the man on the bridge — the 'down the hill' audio and the Bridge Guy image came from her phone. Investigators credited her as the case's key witness.

questions.q: What physical evidence at the scene was linked to Richard Allen?
questions.explain: An unspent .40-caliber round found between the girls was determined by examiners to have cycled through Allen's pistol.

questions.q: When was Richard Allen arrested?
questions.explain: Five and a half years after the murders — October 2022. He had lived and worked in Delphi the entire time.

questions.q: Where did Allen work in Delphi?
questions.explain: He worked at the CVS in town — and had even processed photos for the community, a detail that unsettled Delphi when it surfaced.

questions.q: What was the outcome of Allen's 2024 trial?
questions.explain: In November 2024 a jury convicted him on all counts; he was sentenced to 130 years.

quizzes.title: Infamous & Unsolved
quizzes.description: Five cases, zero convictions. How well do you know the files that never closed?

questions.q: D.B. Cooper hijacked a Boeing 727 in 1971 and vanished with how much?
questions.explain: $200,000 in twenties. In 1980 a boy found $5,800 of it decaying on the Columbia River shore — the case's only confirmed physical lead.

questions.q: Which Zodiac cipher was finally cracked in 2020?
questions.explain: A trio of amateur codebreakers solved the 340 after 51 years. It contained no identifying information — just taunts.

questions.q: The Black Dahlia was the press name for which victim?
questions.explain: Elizabeth Short, found in Leimert Park, Los Angeles in January 1947. The case file remains open with LAPD.

questions.q: What was stolen in the 1990 Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum heist?
questions.explain: Two men dressed as police took 13 works, including Vermeer's The Concert. The empty frames still hang in the galleries.

questions.q: Jack the Ripper's murders took place in which London district?
questions.explain: Whitechapel, autumn 1888. More than a century of suspects later, no attribution has ever held up to scrutiny.

quizzes.title: Forensics 101
quizzes.description: The lab fundamentals — what the acronyms, patterns, and timelines actually mean when a case hits the bench.

questions.q: CODIS, the FBI's DNA system, stands for what?
questions.explain: The Combined DNA Index System links local, state, and national DNA profiles — a hit can connect crimes decades and states apart.

questions.q: Which fingerprint pattern is the most common?
questions.explain: Loops appear in roughly 60-65 percent of prints; arches are the rarest of the three basic patterns.

questions.q: Rigor mortis is typically fully developed about how long after death?
questions.explain: Onset begins within a few hours and full rigor lands around the 12-hour mark, then passes — one of several clocks examiners read together.

questions.q: Mitochondrial DNA traces which line of inheritance?
questions.explain: mtDNA passes from mother to child, which is why it's used on degraded remains and maternal-line identifications.

questions.q: 'Chain of custody' refers to what?
options: The order of witnesses at trial
questions.explain: Every transfer of evidence gets logged. One undocumented gap and a defense attorney can get the whole exhibit tossed.

quizzes.title: Caught by Technology
quizzes.description: Five endings written by metadata, databases, and one very bad computer decision.

questions.q: What finally identified BTK in 2005?
options: Metadata on a floppy disk he mailed
questions.explain: Dennis Rader asked police if a floppy disk could be traced. They said no. The deleted file's metadata pointed to his church — and to 'Dennis'.

questions.q: The Golden State Killer was identified in 2018 using what?
options: Genetic genealogy on a public database
questions.explain: Investigators built family trees from a crime-scene profile uploaded to GEDmatch, then narrowed to Joseph James DeAngelo and confirmed with discarded DNA.

questions.q: The 'Grim Sleeper' case in LA broke open thanks to what technique?
questions.explain: A familial search flagged a close relative's profile; that led to Lonnie Franklin Jr., confirmed by DNA lifted from a slice of pizza.

questions.q: Silk Road founder Ross Ulbricht was arrested in a library because...
options: Agents needed his laptop open and unlocked
questions.explain: The FBI staged a distraction and grabbed the laptop mid-session — encryption never got the chance to lock.

questions.q: Before his arrest, the Golden State Killer was known by which combined moniker?
questions.explain: East Area Rapist / Original Night Stalker — two crime waves only conclusively linked by DNA in 2001, years before the name Golden State Killer stuck.

quizzes.title: True Crime History
quizzes.description: Before podcasts, there were headlines. Five questions from the cases that built the genre.

questions.q: Bruno Hauptmann was convicted in the Lindbergh kidnapping partly through...
questions.explain: The ransom was paid in soon-to-be-recalled gold certificates. Spending them is what put Hauptmann on the map — along with wood evidence matching his attic.

questions.q: What finally convicted Al Capone in 1931?
questions.explain: Eleven years for tax evasion. The murders were never successfully pinned on him — the ledgers were.

questions.q: The 1962 Alcatraz escapees left the island on...
questions.explain: Frank Morris and the Anglin brothers built a raft and life vests from prison raincoats. The FBI closed its file in 1979; the Marshals' file is still open.

questions.q: Who saved Leopold and Loeb from the death penalty in 1924?
questions.explain: Darrow had them plead guilty and argued against death itself for two days straight. The judge gave life plus 99 years.

questions.q: H.H. Holmes operated during which Chicago event?
questions.explain: His 'Murder Castle' hotel ran during the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition. He confessed to 27 murders, though the true count is still debated.
